title: David's Census, the Plague, and the Threshing Floor
summary: Incited by Satan, David orders a census of Israel over Joab's objections, and God judges it as sin. Offered three punishments, David chooses to fall into the LORD's hands, and a plague kills seventy thousand. When the angel of the LORD stands over Jerusalem, God stops the destruction, and David buys Ornan's threshing floor at full price, builds an altar, and God answers with fire from heaven.
story: After chapters of blessing and victory, the Chronicler tells the one sin of David he chooses to narrate at length. It is not the Bathsheba affair but a census, and it matters because of where it leads. The story ends at the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, where judgment stops and an altar is built. The next verse (22:1) makes the point explicit: here shall be the house of the LORD God. The temple's site is chosen not in a moment of triumph but in a moment of sin, repentance, and mercy. Everything that follows in 1 Chronicles 22-29, the preparations for the temple, flows from this place.
historical:
The chapter parallels 2 Samuel 24, with notable differences. Samuel says the anger of the LORD burned against Israel and He incited David; Chronicles names Satan as the one who incited him (see the hard question below). Joab's totals differ: 2 Samuel 24:9 gives 800,000 for Israel and 500,000 for Judah, where Chronicles gives 1,100,000 and 470,000 and adds that Levi and Benjamin were not counted. Samuel's list of punishments has seven years of famine in the Hebrew text, though the Greek translation (the Septuagint) has three, matching Chronicles. The price differs as well: fifty shekels of silver for the threshing floor and oxen in 2 Samuel 24:24, six hundred shekels of gold for the site here. Some explain the price difference as the smaller sum for the floor and oxen and the larger for the whole surrounding site; others see the Chronicler emphasizing the temple site's value.

The threshing floor lay on the hill north of the old city of David, which 2 Chronicles 3:1 identifies with Mount Moriah, the name of the region where Abraham was sent to offer Isaac (Genesis 22:2). Ornan (Araunah in Samuel) was a Jebusite, one of the city's pre-Israelite inhabitants, still holding property after David's conquest.
cultural:
In the ancient Near East a census was usually taken for taxation or military conscription, and the numbers here are of men who drew the sword. It asserted the king's control over the people's strength. Exodus 30:12 required a ransom payment at a census so that no plague would come, which suggests that counting Israel was understood as spiritually dangerous. Joab's objection, are they not all servants of my lord, may hint that the census treated God's people as the king's resource.

A threshing floor was a flat, hard surface, often on high ground to catch the wind, where harvested grain was beaten out and winnowed. Oxen pulled heavy sledges studded with stones or metal across the stalks. Ornan offers the oxen for sacrifice and the wooden sledges for fuel. Sackcloth, a rough goat-hair fabric, was worn as a sign of mourning and repentance. Fire from heaven consuming an offering was a sign of divine acceptance, as at the first tabernacle sacrifice (Leviticus 9:24) and on Mount Carmel (1 Kings 18:38).
literary: The story moves in a clear arc: sin (verses 1-6), judgment (verses 7-14), mercy and intercession (verses 15-17), and atonement at a new altar (verses 18-30). David is at his worst and at his best in the same chapter. He overrules good advice, then confesses fully, I have sinned greatly. He chooses God's hand over human hands because His mercies are very great. When the angel appears, he offers himself in place of the people: these sheep, what have they done? His refusal of Ornan's gift is the chapter's most famous line: I will not take for the LORD what belongs to you, nor will I offer burnt offerings that cost me nothing. The closing verses explain why this altar, not the tabernacle at Gibeon, became the place of worship.

outline.t: Satan incites the census; Joab objects and counts
God's displeasure, David's confession, three choices
The plague, the angel, and David's intercession
David buys Ornan's threshing floor at full price
The altar, fire from heaven, and the sword sheathed

doctrines.note: David names his sin without excuse and takes responsibility as the shepherd whose sin brought harm on the flock. Genuine repentance here includes confession, submission to God's discipline, and costly worship.

The plague stops at an altar where burnt offerings and peace offerings are made and God answers with fire. The chapter shows sacrifice as God's appointed way to turn away judgment, and it locates the temple, Israel's center of atonement, on that spot.

Satan incites, David chooses, and God judges and relents. The chapter holds these agents together without explaining every connection, and the parallel in Samuel attributes the incitement to God's anger, pointing to God's rule even over evil (see the hard question).
The census was evil in God's sight, and judgment fell. Yet the LORD saw and relented, and said Enough. Judgment in this chapter is real but is not God's last word.

words.note: Satan, adversary or accuser. Elsewhere the word can describe a human opponent or an angel standing in someone's way (Numbers 22:22). In Job 1-2 and Zechariah 3 it appears with the article, the satan, a heavenly accuser. Here it appears without the article, which many read as a personal name, Satan, while others translate an adversary.

Rachamim, compassion or mercies, related to the word for womb. David chooses the LORD's hand because His mercies are very great (verse 13). The word suggests a deep, almost bodily tenderness, and David stakes everything on it.

Nacham, here to relent (verse 15). When used of God it describes a change in his declared action in response to repentance or intercession, not a change in his character. The LORD saw and relented from the calamity.

Goren, threshing floor. It appears five times in the chapter, marking the site where judgment halts and worship begins. Threshing floors in Scripture are places of harvest and decision, and this one becomes the foundation of the temple.

christ: The chapter shows a king who offers himself in place of his people, let Your hand fall upon me, and a sacrifice at a costly altar that stops judgment. Christians see here a pattern fulfilled in Christ, the son of David who is also the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11), and whose sacrifice turns away judgment in a way David's could not. The temple built on this threshing floor later becomes, in the New Testament, a figure of Christ's own body (John 2:19-21). The location of the site on Moriah links it with Abraham's offering of Isaac, another story of a substitute provided by God. These connections are typological, patterns the New Testament and Christian tradition trace, rather than predictions stated in the chapter.

hard.q: Who incited David to take the census: God (2 Samuel 24:1) or Satan (1 Chronicles 21:1)? And why was a census sinful?
hard.a:
2 Samuel 24:1 says the LORD's anger burned against Israel and He incited David; this chapter says Satan incited him. Several explanations are offered. Many interpreters see both as true at different levels: God permitted or used Satan's temptation to accomplish a judgment he had already determined, much as in Job 1-2, where the accuser acts only with God's permission. Others see a development in Israel's theology after the exile, with the Chronicler making explicit a heavenly adversary who stands behind evil, protecting God from being seen as the author of sin. Some take the Hebrew here as an adversary, perhaps a human opponent whose threat prompted David's census. All agree the Chronicler still holds David responsible: David himself confesses I have sinned greatly.

The Bible doesn't say plainly why the census was sinful. Suggestions include pride and trust in military numbers rather than in God, a failure to pay the ransom that Exodus 30:12 required, and treating God's people as the king's possession. Joab's objection points toward the first and last.

questions: David said he would not offer burnt offerings that cost me nothing. What does costless worship look like, and what would costly worship look like for you?
David chose to fall into God's hands rather than human hands because God's mercies are very great. When have you found God's mercy more trustworthy than people's?
The temple site was chosen at the place of David's worst failure and God's mercy. How might places of failure become places of worship?
